We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

The central question is whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can faithfully reconstruct activations when a single neuron is simultaneously a high-weight participant in multiple learned features — a condition called high-activation polysemanticity — without the L1 sparsity penalty systematically suppressing the weaker of those co-activated features. SAEs are trained to decompose residual stream or MLP activations into sparse linear combinations of dictionary features, but the L1 penalty that enforces sparsity doesn't distinguish between a feature being genuinely absent versus being present at low magnitude underneath a dominant co-activating feature; both get driven toward zero. The expert worry, invisible to beginners, is that reconstruction error isn't uniformly distributed: it concentrates precisely in the regime where polysemantic neurons fire strongly, because the high-activation feature "wins" the competition for sparsity budget, and the suppressed features vanish from the reconstruction even though they were causally active in the forward pass. This creates a systematic blind spot — downstream interpretability claims built on SAE feature attribution will look locally coherent (the dominant feature explains most variance) while silently missing the suppressed features that may be doing the mechanistically interesting work, such as gating, modulation, or carrying syntactic vs. semantic content in parallel. The practical stakes are high: if you use SAE reconstructions to steer or ablate features, you're operating on a lossy compression of the true activation geometry, and suppressed features may re-emerge or cause unexpected behavior when you intervene.

When two dictionary features f₁ (dominant) and f₂ (suppressed) have decoder vectors with cosine similarity θ, the L1 penalty creates an effective interference term: activating f₂ at coefficient c₂ contributes c₂·cos(θ) toward reconstructing the f₁ direction, which the optimizer can partially achieve "for free" by raising c₁ instead — so the marginal L1 cost of attributing signal to f₂ rises relative to simply inflating c₁, and f₂'s coefficient gets shrunk preferentially. The suppression is therefore not symmetric: when f₁ and f₂ are nearly orthogonal (cos θ ≈ 0), suppression is minimal because inflating c₁ doesn't help reconstruct f₂'s direction at all, and the optimizer has no incentive to trade one for the other; but as cos θ increases toward ~0.3–0.5 — the range Elhage et al. (2022) identified as the typical inter-feature angle in superposition — suppression becomes severe because the dominant feature's direction partially "covers" the suppressed one. Anthropic's April 2024 SAE scaling work (Bricken et al.) implicitly surfaces this: reconstruction loss on held-out polysemantic neurons plateaus despite dictionary expansion, which is consistent with suppression being angle-determined rather than capacity-determined — adding more features doesn't fix the problem if the new features land near existing dominant ones. The implication for polysemanticity degree is non-linear: a neuron encoding k features doesn't produce k-fold suppression uniformly, but rather a suppression profile determined by the full Gram matrix of those k decoder vectors, where features that cluster angularly suffer compounding suppression while near-orthogonal minority features partially escape. This means severity scales worst not with raw polysemanticity count but with angular clustering among the co-encoded features — a neuron encoding 5 tightly clustered features is more destructive to SAE reconstruction than one encoding 10 near-orthogonal features, a distinction the standard polysemanticity metrics (e.g., participation ratio) don't capture.

The L1 objective creates a competing pressure: on one hand, high cosine similarity between decoder vectors increases suppression and reconstruction loss, which should push features apart; on the other hand, the encoder's job is to correctly attribute co-activated signal, and if two features genuinely co-occur frequently in the training data, keeping their decoder vectors somewhat aligned reduces the per-sample reconstruction cost even at the price of occasional suppression — so the optimizer faces a data-dependent tension, not a clean repulsion force. The theoretical prediction is therefore that L1 SAEs will not spontaneously produce uniform angular separation; instead they'll produce a geometry that reflects co-occurrence statistics, with frequently co-activated features drifting toward moderate cosine similarity (~0.2–0.4) as a stable compromise, and only rarely co-activated features being pushed toward orthogonality. Empirically, Bricken et al. (2023) on one-layer MLP SAEs and Wright & Sharkey (2024) on residual stream SAEs both report that learned dictionary matrices have a non-trivial fraction of feature pairs with cosine similarity in the 0.2–0.5 range — far from the near-orthogonal geometry you'd expect if L1 were acting as an effective repulsion force. More tellingly, "feature splitting" under dictionary expansion (a well-documented SAE phenomenon) produces daughter features with high mutual cosine similarity (~0.6–0.8 in some reported cases), which directly contradicts the hypothesis that L1 training self-organizes toward angular diversity; the optimizer finds it cheaper to split a high-frequency feature into overlapping sub-features than to enforce orthogonality. The practical implication is sharp: L1 training has no mechanism analogous to a Coulomb repulsion in feature space — the geometry is demand-driven, not uniformity-driven — which means high-cosine-similarity clusters will persist wherever the underlying data distribution produces correlated features, and suppression in those clusters is a structural artifact of the training objective rather than a fixable initialization problem.

The key insight is that L1's suppression problem is specifically caused by the continuous shrinkage it applies to all coefficients — the penalty is always "on," so small legitimate activations get squeezed toward zero proportionally to how much their decoder vectors overlap with dominant features. L0 approximations and JumpSAE's jump ReLU attack this at the root: rather than penalizing coefficient magnitude continuously, they penalize the count of active features, which means once a feature clears a learned threshold it contributes its full coefficient without magnitude shrinkage — Rajamanoharan et al. (2024) report that JumpSAEs achieve the same sparsity levels as L1 SAEs with meaningfully lower L2 reconstruction error on Gemma-2 residual stream activations, which is consistent with reduced suppression of sub-dominant features. The straight-through L0 estimator (as in... Gao et al. 2024's OpenAI SAE work) shows a similar pattern: by using a hard thresholding operation in the forward pass with a surrogate gradient in the backward pass, it eliminates the continuous shrinkage bias, and the resulting dictionaries show less pathological cosine similarity clustering in the 0.3–0.5 range compared to matched L1 baselines — though neither paper frames this explicitly in terms of suppression dynamics. GroupLasso is a different animal: it penalizes groups of features jointly, which could in principle reduce inter-group suppression by encouraging clean group boundaries, but in practice SAE implementations don't have a principled grouping prior that maps onto polysemanticity structure, so GroupLasso tends to produce within-group suppression rather than eliminating it. The honest answer on decoupling is no current objective fully solves it: JumpSAE and L0 reduce magnitude shrinkage but don't change the fundamental geometry problem — if two decoder vectors have cosine similarity 0.5, the encoder still faces ambiguity about how to attribute shared signal between them during the forward pass, and that ambiguity produces suppression errors regardless of whether the penalty is L1 or threshold-based; the geometry problem requires architectural changes (e.g., non-linear decoder, iterative inference), not just a different sparsity norm.

The canonical failure mode is coherence-induced oscillation: when two decoder vectors have cosine similarity θ ≈ 0.3–0.5, each iterative residual update partially "blames" the current residual on whichever feature wasn't selected in the previous pass, causing the algorithm to alternately activate f₁ and f₂ rather than converging to a stable joint activation — this is the sparse recovery analog of the restricted isometry property (RIP) violation, and it's well-characterized in the compressed sensing literature (Candès & Tao, 2005) as the regime where greedy pursuit algorithms like OMP provably fail to recover the correct support. In the SAE context specifically, naive iterative residual decoding (encode → decode → re-encode residual → accumulate) compounds this because the encoder was trained on single-pass inputs, not on residuals from a partial reconstruction — so the encoder's learned thresholds and weight matrices are systematically miscalibrated for the residual distribution, causing it to over-activate features in early passes and then fail to suppress them in later passes when the residual shrinks. A second failure mode is coefficient drift under accumulation: because each pass adds new feature activations to a running sum without revisiting earlier coefficients, errors from pass 1 (e.g., c₁ inflated to cover f₂'s direction) are never corrected, and subsequent passes try to explain a residual that has already been distorted by the earlier over-attribution — this is distinct from oscillation and occurs even when the algorithm does select the correct features, producing coefficient vectors that sum to the right direction but with individually wrong magnitudes. ISTA (Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm) and LISTA (its learned version, Gregor & LeCun 2010) handle this correctly by updating all coefficients jointly at each step with a proximal gradient step, rather than greedily accumulating new ones — but translating LISTA into the SAE setting requires unrolling the full optimization trajectory during training, which is computationally expensive and introduces its own instability when the dictionary is large (d ~ 10⁴–10⁵ features). The deepest problem is that convergence guarantees for iterative sparse recovery require the dictionary's mutual coherence μ = max_{i≠j} |⟨fᵢ, fⱼ⟩| to satisfy μ < 1/(2k-1) for recovering k-sparse signals — for k=5 co-active features this requires μ < 0.11, but empirically measured SAE dictionaries routinely have μ in the 0.4–0.7 range for the most polysemantic neurons, placing them firmly outside the regime where any iterative algorithm is guaranteed to converge to the correct solution.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-3571)

The distinction is both mathematically meaningful and practically consequential: non-unique decomposition is a property of the activation vector and dictionary together — it means there exist multiple sparse coefficient vectors that reconstruct the activation equally well, so no algorithm could identify the "correct" one without additional constraints — whereas algorithmic failure means a unique correct decomposition exists but the SAE's encoder doesn't find it, producing a suboptimal solution with higher reconstruction error or wrong support. The Donoho-Elad uniqueness theorem (2003) gives a precise criterion: a k-sparse decomposition is unique if and only if k < (1 + 1/μ)/2, where μ is the dictionary's mutual coherence — so for μ = 0.5 (well within empirically observed SAE ranges), uniqueness is only guaranteed for k < 1.5, meaning any activation requiring 2 or more co-active features is potentially in the non-unique regime. Empirically distinguishing the two failure modes requires a ground-truth reference that SAE training doesn't provide, but there are tractable proxies: if you run multiple SAE training runs with different random seeds and find that the learned feature assignments for a specific polysemantic neuron are inconsistent across runs (different features activated, similar reconstruction error), that's strong evidence of non-uniqueness rather than algorithmic failure, because algorithmic failure would produce consistently wrong-but-similar errors. Conversely, if reconstruction error is high and consistent across seeds while ablation experiments show that no combination of dictionary features can explain the neuron's causal behavior on downstream tasks, you're looking at algorithmic failure — the unique decomposition exists but the trained encoder can't reach it, likely due to the coherence-induced optimization landscape issues described previously. Bricken et al. (2023) implicitly encounter this when they note that some neurons show "unresolvable" reconstruction error even with very large dictionaries — the plateau in reconstruction loss despite capacity expansion is more consistent with non-uniqueness (the true decomposition isn't stably identifiable) than with simple underfitting. The practical implication is sharp: interpretability claims built on SAE feature attribution should be treated with fundamentally different epistemic status depending on which failure mode dominates — algorithmic failure is potentially fixable with better training, but non-uniqueness means the SAE is being asked to solve an ill-posed problem, and any particular solution it produces is one of many equally valid ones with no principled basis for preferring it.

The most principled additional constraint is causal consistency: rather than requiring only that the SAE reconstruct activations accurately, require that each dictionary feature's coefficient predict a specific causal footprint in downstream computation — if feature f₂ is genuinely active, ablating its direction should produce a predictable change in logits or attention patterns, whereas a spurious alternative decomposition would assign coefficient mass to f₂ without that causal signature. This is the logic behind Marks et al.'s (2024) activation editing experiments and the broader "causal scrubbing" framework (Chan et al., 2022) — causal consistency as a constraint transforms the ill-posed reconstruction problem into a better-posed identification problem, because among all sparse decompositions with equivalent L2 error, only one (or a small equivalence class) will have the right causal structure. A second candidate is temporal or contextual smoothness: if the same neuron fires across a sequence of related inputs (e.g., a sentence with consistent syntactic structure), the correct decomposition should vary smoothly in coefficient space rather than jumping discontinuously between alternative sparse solutions — this is an inductive bias that could be enforced via a regularizer penalizing coefficient variance across semantically similar inputs, though no major SAE implementation currently does this. A third constraint is cross-layer consistency: if feature f₂ represents a genuine semantic concept, its activation coefficient in layer L should be predictable from SAE decompositions of earlier layers via the residual stream — Lindsey et al. (2024) gesture toward this in their cross-layer SAE work, finding that features with high cross-layer predictability correspond better to human-interpretable concepts, which is indirect evidence that cross-layer consistency selects for the "correct" decomposition among non-unique alternatives. The uncomfortable truth is that the constraint most consistent with the linear representation hypothesis — that features are directions in activation space used linearly by downstream circuits — is precisely sparsity plus causal consistency, but these two together are still insufficient to guarantee uniqueness when μ is high; you need the network to have actually implemented a sparse code, which is an empirical claim about the network's inductive biases during training (e.g., from implicit regularization, dropout, or weight decay) rather than something the SAE can impose post-hoc.

Immediately after an MoE routing layer, the residual stream activation for a given token is the sum of the pre-MoE residual plus the outputs of whichever k experts were selected (typically k=2 in Mixtral-style routing, k=1 or k=2 in Gemini MoE configurations) — and because each expert has its own weight matrix operating in a different functional subspace, the resulting vector is a superposition of expert-specific representations that were never jointly optimized to be linearly separable. Cross-layer consistency as an identifying constraint breaks down here in a specific way: the SAE at layer L+1 (post-MoE) is trying to find a decomposition consistent with layer L (pre-MoE), but the intervening expert computation has rotated, scaled, and mixed the feature directions in ways that are token-routing-dependent — so the same concept represented at layer L may project onto completely different directions at layer L+1 depending on which experts fired, making the cross-layer predictability signal noisy or zero even for genuine features. Empirically, Gao et al. (2024) and the Mixtral interpretability work from EleutherAI both note that SAE reconstruction loss spikes at post-MoE residual stream positions compared to attention-only positions, which is consistent with the post-MoE activation geometry being harder to decompose — but neither paper isolates whether this is due to increased polysemanticity, expert mixture incompatibility, or simply higher activation variance. The deeper problem is that MoE routing introduces conditional independence structure that a single flat SAE dictionary can't represent: token A routed through experts {1,3} and token B routed through experts {2,4} may have superficially similar residual stream activations (similar L2 norm, similar projection onto shared directions) but completely different causal provenance, so any decomposition that ignores routing identity is conflating causally distinct representations. A principled fix would require routing-conditioned SAEs — separate dictionaries per expert combination, or a mixture-of-SAEs architecture where the router's hard decision gates which sub-dictionary is applied — but this combinatorially explodes for large k and E (number of experts), and no published work has demonstrated that routing-conditioned SAEs recover cross-layer consistency in the post-MoE regime.
